meta.title: Drake Equation / Fermi Paradox
meta.description: N = R* · fp · ne · fl · fi · fc · L with order-of-magnitude (log-uniform) priors, after Sandberg, Drexler & Ord's 'Dissolving the Fermi Paradox'. The point of the exercise: with honest uncertainty, the MEDIAN number of communicating civilizations can be modest while the MEAN is enormous — and P(we are alone) is not small.

nodes.title: Star formation rate (stars/yr)
nodes.notes: Rate of star formation in the Milky Way. Astronomy pins this reasonably well; the range covers disagreement across surveys.

nodes.title: Fraction of stars with planets
nodes.notes: Post-Kepler this is close to 1; the lower bound is conservative.

nodes.title: Habitable planets per system
nodes.notes: Planets per planetary system that could support life.

nodes.title: Fraction where life emerges
nodes.notes: Abiogenesis probability given a habitable planet — genuinely unknown across orders of magnitude. This and f_i dominate the answer (check the tornado once sensitivity lands).

nodes.title: Fraction developing intelligence
nodes.notes: Given life, probability that intelligence evolves.

nodes.title: Fraction that communicate
nodes.notes: Given intelligence, probability of detectable technology.

nodes.title: Civilization lifetime (years)
nodes.notes: How long a communicating civilization remains detectable — from a century to ten billion years.

nodes.title: Communicating civilizations in the galaxy
nodes.expr: R_star * f_p * n_e * f_l * f_i * f_c * L

nodes.title: P(we are effectively alone)
nodes.notes: Probability that fewer than one other communicating civilization exists — the 'dissolved' Fermi paradox is that this is sizable even when the mean of N is huge.
